The net effect is that while the Indian economy was reportedly recording robust growth according to statistics put out by the Government, farmers were committing suicide. While India boasted of healthy foreign exchange reserves, exports were falling. Employment opportunities were dwindling. Huge sums of money were apparently spent on the Social Sector by the UPA Government. Yet, India languishes at the bottom of the Human Development Index at the global level. It is indeed a reflection of the paradoxical state of affairs in the country that while India boasts of some of the world’s richest people, some of the districts of the country are comparable to sub-Saharan Africa - one of the poorest and most underdeveloped regions of the world.

Yet, India continues to remain intact and out-perform many economies at the global level. And for this the credit must go to the average Indian -- farmers, teachers, salaried employees, artisans, labourers, workers, government employees, self-employed, students, senior citizens, community leaders and of course the lady of the house.

For three successive decades beginning from 1980, India has been witnessing a robust growth in excess of six percent. Nevertheless, India continues to languish at the bottom of the Human Development Index (HDI) at the international level. The ignominy is best captured by the fact that India is ranked 132 amongst about 180 countries, while several of our war-torn, tiny neighbours are ranked above us. Once again, this piece of statistics cruelly exposes the claim of the UPA Government about its concern for the common man (aam aadmi). India ranks poorly in food consumption, fresh water consumption, literacy, nutrition levels, sanitation, education and low in primary healthcare and high in infant mortality and death during child birth. These need to be tackled by a combination of increased allocations; proper governance and devolution of powers.
